Editorial framing AI-drafted, status:draft, pending Wilson's curation. [v2 migration 2026-09-10: gravity/synthesis moved under tracks.complementary (verified against that track's first reading, not assumed); the other track has firstReading only, pending Phase 4b authoring.] [Phase 4b 2026-09-10, Opus: Gospel doors gained a Glossa (Migne 13:30) witness; semicontinuous half authored — gravity, synthesis, three Genesis 28 doors — from src/turn_pull.py output.]
trap: The parable gets read as a shrug ("don't judge anything") or, flipped, as a mandate for the zealous to start pulling weeds — purging the church, the family, the world of the wrong people. Both miss that the restraint is the King's command and the sorting is the King's alone.
hinge: The weeds are real — the enemy's own work, not to be pretended away — and you are forbidden to pull them, because your hands cannot tell wheat from weed without tearing up both. Real evil, real judgment, and your task in the meantime is patience, not harvest.

doors.claim: You are not the reaper — pulling the weeds now would tear up wheat with them, so the command is a hard patience that leaves room for the weed to become wheat.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Room for repentance is left, and we are warned not to cut off a brother hastily, since one who today is corrupted by error may tomorrow be set right.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: This the Lord spoke to forbid any putting to death; for we ought not to kill even a heretic, since so a never-ending war would be brought into the world.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: As between the cockle and the wheat, so long as it is in the blade, there is little difference: so the Lord admonishes us not to judge concerning a doubtful thing, which the Lord in the day of judgment will condemn not by suspicion, but manifestly.

doors.say: Your hands are not steady enough to weed God's field; the patience that galls you is mercy leaving a door open.
doors.do: Name one person they have already written off as a weed, and ask them to keep the door of repentance open instead of uprooting.

doors.claim: The weeds came in the unguarded hour, sown by an enemy and not by God — which both names the origin of evil and calls the sleepers to wake.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: "While men slept" — while the leaders of the Church lay in supineness, and after the Apostles had fallen into the sleep of death, then the enemy came.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: While men slept — they ought to have watched; the Lord of the field never sleeps. An enemy has done this: a plain answer to the great question of the origin of evil.

doors.say: The weeds in your life and your church are not from the hand of God — they were sown in a sleeping hour, and the call is to wake.
doors.do: Point to one unguarded place — a habit, a relationship, a corner of the church — where vigilance has lapsed, and watch there again.

doors.claim: The mixed field is not the last word — there is a harvest, a real and final sorting that belongs to God, where the weeds are bound and the righteous shine like the sun.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: Behold the love of God: ready to show mercy, slow to punish. When he sows, he sows himself; when he punishes, he punishes by others — by the angels.

witnesses.author: Remigius of Auxerre
witnesses.reading: The harvest is the day of judgment, when the good are parted from the evil by the ministry of angels; the righteous, who now shine for an example, shall then shine as the sun.

doors.say: Leave the verdict to the harvest — it is coming, it is God's, and the wheat will shine in it.
doors.do: Turn anxious or vengeful hearts from rendering verdicts now to entrusting the harvest to God — and to living as wheat.

complementary.gravity: Wisdom says God judges with mildness and great forbearance, and so teaches his people that the righteous must be kind; Paul hears the whole creation groaning in hope; and Jesus tells of a field where wheat and weeds grow tangled until harvest. The nerve: how to live faithfully in a world — and a church — that will not sort cleanly into good and evil.

synthesis.convergence: The readings show a sovereignty that looks like forbearance — a God who judges with mildness and teaches his people to be kind (Wisdom 12), who abounds in steadfast love (Psalm 86), who waits with a groaning creation that hopes for what it cannot yet see (Romans 8) — over a field where wheat and weeds grow tangled until harvest.
synthesis.claim: The God who could uproot every weed chooses patience and kindness instead — and asks the same costly patience of you.
synthesis.here: For people quick to sort the world (and the church) into the righteous and the villains, the move is the hard patience of hope: leave the harvest to God, extend to the 'weeds' the mildness God extends to you, and wait — with the whole groaning creation — for a verdict that is not yours to render.

doors.landing: Surely the Lord is in this place
doors.claim: Jacob meets God where he least expected to, on the run and sleeping rough: the presence was there before he knew it.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: We sometimes meet with God there, where we little thought of meeting with him. He is there where we did not think he had been, is found there where we asked not for him.

doors.say: Jacob didn't find God at the altar he'd planned to build. He found God on the road he was fleeing down.
doors.do: Ask them to name the place in their week they assume God is absent, and to go there this week expecting otherwise.

doors.claim: To a man leaving home with nothing, God speaks promise before any demand: presence on the road, and a way back.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: He was now going as an exile into a place far distant, but God promiseth him to bring him again to this land. He seemed to be forsaken of all his friends, but God gives him this assurance, I will not leave thee.

doors.say: Before Jacob has done a single thing right, God promises to go with him and bring him home.
doors.do: Invite anyone in a season of leaving — a move, a loss, an exile of any kind — to carry that promise with them by name.

doors.claim: The angels go both ways: the life of faith climbs toward God in prayer and comes back down in compassion for the weak.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Jacob signifies preachers, who not only, by contemplating, seek after the head of the Church, that is, Christ, but descend by compassion to his members: which the angels ascending and descending show forth.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: The angels are active spirits, continually ascending and descending; they rest not day nor night.

doors.say: The ladder isn't only for going up. Every climb toward God in prayer is meant to come back down to someone who needs you.
doors.do: Pair one practice of prayer this week with one concrete act of care for someone struggling.

semicontinuous.gravity: Jacob, a fugitive with a stone for a pillow, dreams of a ladder between earth and heaven and wakes to say, "Surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not" (Genesis 28); the Psalm finds no place, not even darkness, where God is absent; Paul hears the creation groaning as it waits (Romans 8); and Jesus lets the weeds and the wheat grow together until harvest. The nerve: God is already present in the mixed, unfinished, unlikely place, before we notice.

synthesis.convergence: A fugitive sleeps on a stone and finds the place is the house of God (Genesis 28); the psalmist cannot flee God's presence even into the dark (Psalm 139); Paul hears all creation groaning in labor (Romans 8); and in a field sown with weeds the owner says wait (Matthew 13). Each reading insists that God is at work in the mixed and unfinished place we would rather leave or clean up.
synthesis.claim: The place you are trying to escape or fix may be the place God already is: stop, look, and wait.
synthesis.here: For people who see their church, their family, or their own heart as a weedy field or a wilderness road, the move is Jacob's waking — "surely the Lord is in this place" — before any pulling up or walking away.

subtract: Three doors, three landings — patience (let both grow), vigilance (while they slept), hope-and-warning (the harvest sorts it). Choose one for your people and let the others go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
